questions.question: Which of the following is the correct way to open a file named 'notes.txt' just to read its content?
options: `file = open('notes.txt', 'w')`
`file = read('notes.txt')`
`file = open('notes.txt', 'r')`
`file = open('notes.txt', 'a')`
questions.explanation: To read a file, you use the `open()` function with the `'r'` (read) mode. Note that `'r'` is also the default if you don't specify a mode.

questions.question: What is a major risk of using the `'w'` (Write) mode on a file that already contains data?
options: It will cause a `FileNotFoundError`.
It will add the new data to the end of the existing content.
It will delete (overwrite) all existing content in the file.
It will open the file in read-only mode instead.
questions.explanation: The `'w'` mode is destructive for existing files; it wipes the file clean as soon as it is opened. If you want to keep existing data, you should use `'a'` (Append) mode instead.

questions.question: Why is it considered a best practice to call the `.close()` method?
options: It is the only way to print the file's content.
It deletes the file from the hard drive to save space.
It tells Python which mode to use for the next file.
It frees up system resources and ensures all data is successfully written to the disk.
questions.explanation: Closing the file is like hanging up a phone call; it tells the Operating System that your program is finished with the resource, preventing memory leaks and data corruption.

questions.question: What does `.readline()` return when it reaches the end of a file?
options: None
An empty string `""`
A `StopIteration` error
An empty list `[]`
questions.explanation: When the file pointer reaches the end of the file, `.readline()` returns an empty string. This is often used as a signal in loops to stop reading.

questions.question: Why is iterating over a file object (using a `for` loop) preferred over `.readlines()` for large files?
options: It is the only way to read a file in Python
It automatically sorts the lines alphabetically
It reads one line at a time instead of loading the whole file into memory
It automatically closes the file for you
questions.explanation: Iterating over the file object is 'lazy,' meaning it only loads the current line being processed into memory. `.readlines()` loads the entire file into a list at once, which can crash your program if the file is several gigabytes large.

questions.question: You have just finished reading a file using a `for` loop. If you want to read it again from the top without closing it, what should you do?
options: Call `file_handle.reset()`
Use `file_handle.seek(0)` to move the pointer to the start
Call `.readline()` again; it resets automatically
There is no way to read a file twice
questions.explanation: The file pointer stays at the end of the file after a full read. To go back to the beginning without reopening the file, you use `.seek(0)` to move the pointer back to the byte at index 0.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using the `with` statement when opening files?
options: It makes the file read faster
It automatically closes the file when the block is finished
It prevents the file from being deleted
It allows you to open a file without specifying a mode
questions.explanation: The `with` statement acts as a context manager, ensuring that `file.close()` is called automatically, which prevents memory leaks and file corruption.

questions.question: What happens if an error occurs inside a `with open(...)` block?
options: The file remains open until the computer restarts
The file is corrupted immediately
The file is closed safely
The `with` block ignores the error and continues
questions.explanation: This is a key safety feature. Even if an exception is raised, the context manager's 'exit' logic is triggered, closing the file safely.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct syntax for opening two files simultaneously using a context manager?
options: `with open('f1.txt') as x and open('f2.txt') as y:`
`with open('f1.txt') as x, open('f2.txt') as y:`
`with open('f1.txt', 'f2.txt') as x, y:`
`with open('f1.txt') as x + open('f2.txt') as y:`
questions.explanation: You can manage multiple resources in a single `with` statement by separating the `open()` calls with a comma.

questions.question: What happens if you open an existing file using the `'w'` mode?
options: Python throws an error to prevent data loss
The file is opened and the new data is added to the end
The existing content is deleted and the file starts fresh
The file is opened in read-only mode instead
questions.explanation: Write mode `'w'` is destructive for existing files. It 'truncates' the file, meaning it wipes all current content before you start writing.

questions.question: Which of the following code snippets correctly writes two separate lines to a file?
options: `f.write('Line 1', 'Line 2')`

`f.write('Line 1')
f.write('Line 2')`

`f.write('Line 1\n')
f.write('Line 2\n')`
`f.write('Line 1' + 'Line 2')`
questions.explanation: Because `.write()` does not add newlines automatically, you must explicitly include the `\n` character at the end of your strings to separate lines.

questions.question: If you are building a system to track error messages throughout the day, which mode should you use to open the log file?
options: `'r'` (Read)
`'w'` (Write)
`'a'` (Append)
`'x'` (Execute)
questions.explanation: Append mode `'a'` is ideal for logs because it preserves the existing history and adds new data to the end of the file.
